title: Canada puts more money down on F-35s as fighter review drags on
summary: Canada has made another payment for F-35 components, securing a potential fleet of 48 stealth fighters despite an ongoing review of the original 88-aircraft purchase. The federal government insists…

image.caption: An F-35A Lightning II is on display during an event celebrating its delivery to Germany in Fort Worth, Texas, in September. Canada has recently made another payment on F-35 parts to secure spots on the production line for additional jets. (Shelby Tauber/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada has made another payment for F-35 components, securing a potential fleet of 48 stealth fighters despite an ongoing review of the original 88-aircraft purchase. The federal government insists the payment preserves Canada's place in the production schedule without committing it to additional aircraft as it weighs a competing Swedish proposal.
Ottawa reserves more U.S. production slots, says full order not confirmed
The federal government has put more money down on parts and components for future F-35 fighters, which would potentially bring Canada's fleet up to 48 jets, CBC News has confirmed.
Payment for the "long-lead" items was made recently and is part of the agreement signed with the Pentagon's Joint Project Office, which runs the program.
The decision to make the payment comes even though the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney continues to review whether Canada will buy all 88 fighters, which it originally committed to in 2023.
The first two Canadian F-35 were recently delivered to Luke Air Force base in Arizona where Canadian pilots and maintainers are training on them.
A spokesperson for Defence Minister David McGuinty said the payments were meant to cover the cost of parts that manufacturer Lockheed Martin must buy ahead of assembly.

"The proposed purchase of additional F-35s remains under review, and no decision has been made on the procurement of additional aircraft at this time," Simon Lafortune, the minister's director of communications.

"While this review is underway, Canada will continue to honour its fiscal obligations and maintain its place in line with the Joint Program Office in accordance with agreed schedules, including commitments for long-lead items required to support the fleet.
"This is not a firm financial commitment to purchase additional aircraft, but a reservation by the government of Canada to secure a place in the production schedule."

blocks.text: At the onset of the bitter trade war with the United States last year, Carney's government made the decision to re-examine the planned $27.9-billion purchase of the fighters.
The review by the air force, according to two defence sources, was completed within weeks of being requested.

It has been with cabinet and on Carney's desk as the government has entertained a proposal from Swedish aircraft manufacturer Saab, which wants to fill out the rest of the country's fighter fleet with Gripen-E jets. The company has also proposed setting up an assembly line in Canada.

A government source insisted that Canada wasn't trying to use the F-35 purchase as leverage in trade negotiations with the Trump administration and that the fighters are important for national security.
The Americans, however, don't see it that way.
The U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has repeatedly signalled that the review is an irritant.

Earlier this year, he told CBC News that scaling back the F-35 order would hurt NORAD and force the Americans to buy more of the fighters in order to protect North American airspace. He walked some of those remarks back in a later interview, saying one decision would not break the air defence command.
At the moment, Canada has only committed to buy 16 F-35 aircraft. Money was set aside for that number of aircraft in the 2024 federal budget.
CBC News reported earlier this year that money was set aside in 2025 to secure the parts necessary for another 14 aircraft.
The latest installment for long-lead items brings the total number of aircraft to 48.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
